lessons.title: C# Foundations
lessons.description: Build the small set of C# skills used in SharpRunner's five onboarding trials.
objectives: Identify the basic parts of a small C# program.
Declare int, string, double, and bool variables.
Assign and update values.
Display values with Console.WriteLine.

blocks.text: What is C#?

C# (pronounced C-sharp) is a programming language used to give a computer precise instructions. Developers use it for web services, desktop and mobile apps, cloud systems, and games. A C# program is written as source code, then a compiler checks that code and translates it into instructions the .NET runtime can execute.
Why types matter

C# is strongly typed: every value has a type, and that type controls which operations make sense. Types help the compiler catch mistakes before a program runs—for example, trying to store the word "five" in a whole-number variable.

blocks.label: How to study
blocks.text: Read each example, predict what it displays, and then compare your prediction with the output.
The Awakening introduces the editor and compile flow before later trials ask for text and number values.
Programs and statements

A program is an ordered set of instructions. The computer follows those instructions from top to bottom unless a condition, loop, or method call changes the flow. One complete instruction is usually called a statement.
In the traditional program style below, execution begins in Main. A semicolon ends most statements, parentheses hold information for a method call, and braces group statements into a body.

blocks.title: C# example

items: using System; makes common .NET names available.

Console.WriteLine(...) displays one line.
The semicolon finishes the display statement.

blocks.label: Common mistake
blocks.text: C# is case-sensitive. Console.WriteLine is correct; console.writeline is not.
Declare and assign

A variable is a named storage place for a value your program may need again. Declaration introduces its type and name; assignment uses = to place a value in it. A useful name such as lanterns explains the value better than a vague name such as x.

blocks.value: int lanterns = 5;
blocks.title: Anatomy of a variable statement

items: int → the data type
lanterns → the variable name
= → the assignment operator
5 → the value being stored
; → the end of the statement

blocks.value:
int lanterns = 5;
Console.WriteLine(lanterns);
blocks.title: A whole-number variable

blocks.label: Why is the output 5?
blocks.text: The first statement stores 5 in lanterns. Console.WriteLine then reads the current value of lanterns and displays it.

blocks.title: Updating a value

blocks.label: Remember
blocks.text: Use = to assign a value. The variable name goes on the left and the new value goes on the right.
The Coin Keeper checks that you can represent a required whole-number value.
Choose a type that matches the kind of information you need to store. This matters because C# treats text, whole numbers, decimal numbers, and true/false facts differently.

items: int stores whole numbers, such as 12.
double stores numbers with a decimal part, such as 2.5.
string stores text inside double quotes.
bool stores either true or false.

Console.WriteLine displays a value and then moves to a new line. It can display literal text, a variable, or an expression.

blocks.text: Console.WriteLine displays a value. It does not store that value for later.

An expression combines values and operators to produce a new value. Numeric variables can use + for addition, - for subtraction, * for multiplication, and / for division. C# evaluates the expression on the right before assigning its result.

lessons.title: Arrays
lessons.description: Store, access, change, and traverse related values in one- and two-dimensional arrays.
objectives: Declare and initialize a one-dimensional array.
Access and modify elements by zero-based index.
Use Length and safe index bounds.
Traverse an array with for and foreach.
Declare and access a basic rectangular two-dimensional array.

blocks.text: What is an array?
An array groups a fixed number of related values of the same type under one variable name. Each stored value is an element, and each element has a numbered position called an index.
Why does it exist?

Imagine tracking many lantern powers. Separate variables—lantern1, lantern2, lantern3—force you to repeat nearly identical code and make it difficult to process an unknown number of values. One array keeps the relationship clear and lets a loop visit the whole group.

blocks.title: Without an array

blocks.value: int[] lanterns = { 10, 20, 30 };
blocks.title: Three integers in one array

blocks.value: string[] spirits = { "Aswang", "Tikbalang", "Kapre" };
blocks.title: Three strings in another array

blocks.label: Why use arrays?
blocks.text: Without an array, processing ten related values could require ten variables and ten statements. An array lets one loop process them consistently.
The Lanterns of Malumay and stolen-supplies levels begin with correctly declared arrays.
The square brackets after a type mean 'array of this type.' An initializer between braces supplies the elements in order.

blocks.value:
int[] powers = { 10, 20, 30 };
string[] paths = { "north", "east" };
blocks.title: C# example

items: int is the element type.
[] says the variable holds an array.
powers is the array variable name.
{ 10, 20, 30 } lists the initial elements in order.
The semicolon ends the declaration statement.

blocks.value:
int[] emptySlots = new int[4];
Console.WriteLine(emptySlots.Length);
blocks.title: Create space first

blocks.label: Remember
blocks.text: Every element must be compatible with the array's element type. An int[] cannot contain a string.
The first two array validators check element type, array size, order, and values.
C# array indexes start at 0. Therefore, the first element is index 0, the second is index 1, and the third is index 2.

blocks.caption: Each value sits directly above its index.

Console.WriteLine(powers[1]);

blocks.label: Why is the output 20?
blocks.text: powers[1] asks for the element at index 1. Index 1 is the second position because array indexing begins at 0.

blocks.feedback: 30 is the third element, so its zero-based index is 2.

blocks.text: The Road of Santelmo and Midnight Inventory require reading a specific string by index.
Use an index on the left of = to replace one element. The other elements remain unchanged.

blocks.text: Length is the number of elements. Because indexes begin at 0, the last valid index is Length - 1.

blocks.label: Common mistake
blocks.text: charms[charms.Length] is outside the array. For four elements, Length is 4 but valid indexes are 0 through 3.
A for loop is useful when you need the index. It starts at 0, continues while the index is less than Length, and increases the index after each pass.

foreach gives you each element directly. It is clear when you need every value but do not need to know or change its index.

blocks.label: for or foreach?
blocks.text: Use for when the index matters or you must update by position. Use foreach for straightforward read-only traversal. Neither is always better.

lessons.title: Functions and Methods
lessons.description: Define, call, and combine C# methods with parameters, return values, and safe recursion.
objectives: Define and call a void method.

Distinguish parameters from arguments.
Return and store a value from a method.

blocks.text: What is a method?

A method is a named group of statements that performs one task. In C#, reusable functions defined inside a class or other type are commonly called methods. A clear method name describes the action or result, such as RingBell or CalculatePower.
Why methods matter

Methods let you solve a larger problem as smaller named jobs. You can call the same job more than once, change it in one place, and test it separately. They are useful whenever an action repeats or a calculation deserves a clear name.

blocks.title: A method definition

items: static lets this example call the method from the program's static entry point.
void says the method does not send a value back.
RingBell is the method name.
() is the parameter list; it is empty here.
{ } contains the method body.
Console.WriteLine is the statement that runs after a call.

blocks.value: RingBell();
blocks.title: A method call

blocks.label: Create versus call
blocks.text: Creating the method defines its behavior. Calling the method makes that behavior run.
The First Ritual validator requires both a method definition and a call.
Methods divide a larger program into smaller jobs. They reduce repeated code, make intent easier to read, and let the same behavior run from more than one place.

The word void means the method does not send a result value back to its caller. It can still display output or perform another action.

A non-void method promises to send a value of its declared return type back to the caller. The return keyword supplies that value, and the caller can store it.

blocks.text: Console.WriteLine(50) displays 50. return 50 sends 50 back to the caller so the program can store or calculate with it.

A method can receive inputs, calculate with them, and return one result. This keeps the calculation reusable for different arguments.

A recursive method calls itself. Each call should move toward a base case: a condition that stops further calls.

blocks.title: C# example

items: The method calls itself.

step == 0 is the base case.

blocks.label: Common mistake
blocks.text: Without a reachable base case, calls keep accumulating until the program fails with a stack overflow.

items: Defining a method but never calling it.
Calling a method with the wrong argument type or order.
Declaring a non-void return type but not returning a value.
Trying to use a local variable outside its method.
Printing a result when the caller needs it returned.
Writing recursion without a reachable base case.

blocks.title: Missing return value

blocks.text: This displays 10 but does not satisfy the promise to return an int. The body needs return 10;.

blocks.prompt: What must stop a recursive method?
blocks.feedback: A reachable base case prevents endless recursive calls.

blocks.text: Methods name reusable behavior. Parameters receive inputs, arguments supply them, return sends a result to the caller, and recursion repeats through self-calls until a base case.

items: Definition creates behavior; a call runs it.
void means no result value is returned.
Parameters appear in the definition; arguments appear in the call.
A returned value can be stored by the caller.
Safe recursion must progress toward a base case.

blocks.text: Arrays group same-type values; methods group reusable behavior. Combining them lets one method process any compatible array supplied by its caller.

blocks.title: Method behavior

blocks.label: Integration goal
blocks.text: This module assumes you know indexing, loops, parameters, calls, and return values. It focuses on connecting those ideas.
From caller to method
An int[] parameter can receive a complete one-dimensional integer array. The call passes the array variable name without brackets because it is passing the whole array, not selecting one element.

Arrays are reference types. A method receives a copy of the reference by default; both references point to the same array object. Changing an element through the parameter is visible to the caller.
